title: Swim Don't Sink in a Crowded Curriculum
author: Doing Inclusion
summary: A career-change teacher who moved from secondary maths/science into primary special education recounts how a project to fix disappointing NAPLAN writing results turned into a deeper investigation of why fragmented literacy curricula fail students with disability specifically. Her students' struggles to write even basic sentences did not respond to scaffolding or sentence-first strategies, leading her to trace the real bottlenecks to handwriting automaticity and limited vocabulary, both of which compete for the same finite cognitive capacity a student needs for composing ideas. Her central diagnosis is that schools commonly teach handwriting, vocabulary, reading, and writing as isolated curriculum strands rather than a cohesive, cross-year whole, and that this fragmentation particularly harms students with disability, who risk having material silently omitted because staff assume they "can't" handle it — a constraint she argues becomes self-fulfilling. Her proposed solution treats vocabulary instruction as the connective tissue across subjects and years, citing a need for roughly seven to eight new words daily with about twelve exposures each across hearing, speaking, reading, and writing to build genuine retention. She is explicit that curriculum design is only the first step, arguing implementation support for teachers is where the real difficulty and the real power lie, and frames the entire project through an inclusion lens shaped by her experience assessing a non-speaking student against achievement standards never written with AAC users in mind.
points: Traces students' inability to write even basic sentences to two competing cognitive demands, unautomated handwriting and limited vocabulary, both draining the working memory needed for actually composing ideas.

Argues fragmented, isolated-strand literacy teaching disproportionately harms students with disability, since fragmentation creates opportunities for staff to silently omit content they assume such students "can't" handle.

Cites a specific vocabulary-acquisition benchmark, roughly 7-8 new words daily with about 12 exposures each across hearing, speaking, reading, and writing, as the target a genuinely cohesive cross-year curriculum needs to hit.

Identifies the Australian curriculum's vague achievement standards as concealing a "hidden curriculum" of prerequisite and follow-on knowledge that isn't explicitly written down, especially problematic for assessing non-speaking or AAC-using students.

Insists curriculum design is only the starting point, arguing implementation support that measurably lightens teachers' daily planning load is where a cohesive-curriculum project actually succeeds or fails.
quotes: They struggle to come up with ideas to write even basic sentences. The struggle was not solved with scaffolded supports or carefully sequenced and structured explicit teaching. It wasn't solved by speaking about the sentence first.

For students with disability there is the risk that someone will intentionally not cover certain work because they think the students "can't" do it. Unfortunately I've come to realise that the constraints placed on students by people saying they can't are the very reasons they can't.

My foray into vocabulary suggested students needed to be learning 7-8 words a day with about 12 exposures each across hearing, speaking, reading and writing. That is a big ask and really requires the curriculum to be approached as a cohesive whole.

I have seen what happens when we don't support students with disability with sound fundamental instruction. They go backwards and risk falling into deep learning chasms from which they may never return.

When vocabulary is sequenced and developed across subjects and years with repetition it becomes one of the tools students and teachers can stand on. It can underpin the feelings of success that students need.
This is something i am passionate about because if a student can't access the curriculum it is not a student problem, it is a teacher problem.
